source.title: Neural Networks Efficiently Learn Low-Dimensional Representations with SGD
source.authors: Alireza Mousavi-Hosseini; Sejun Park; M. Girotti; Ioannis Mitliagkas; Murat A. Erdogdu

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper proves bounds on the generalization gap and relates them to convergence toward a low-dimensional principal subspace, using a theoretical teacher–student setting rather than the versions’ empirical interventions.
record.gate_note: The paper studies online SGD on two-layer networks with Gaussian inputs and teacher-generated targets. Its generalization-gap bound is a theorem, not an empirical test of random-label memorization or the listed architecture, optimizer, batch-size, dropout, sharpness, or memorized-example claims. It does not report an experiment comparing training and test error on natural versus random labels.
record.test_reason: The study proves representation-learning, generalization-gap and compression bounds for Gaussian teacher–student models trained with online SGD and weight decay. None establishes or refutes V1–V8. In particular, a width-independent upper bound does not establish decreasing test error beyond interpolation.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors additionally establish learnability of monotone single-index targets with nearly linear-in-d sample complexity, yielding a separation from rotationally invariant kernel methods. Their guarantees require Gaussian inputs and appropriate weight decay; simultaneous training of both layers remains future work.
record.recipe_differences: Theoretical two-layer teacher–student analysis with Gaussian inputs and explicit L2 weight decay; no random-label memorization experiment or natural-label benchmark comparison.
record.method_sensitivity: The generalization-gap bound depends on the number k of teacher directions, input dimension d, iteration count T, step-size schedule, regularization and loss truncation.

fits_no_version.finding: Theorem 5 establishes a width-independent generalization-gap upper bound using approximate convergence to the teacher's principal subspace.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under the stated Gaussian teacher–student assumptions, online SGD with appropriate weight decay admits a generalization-gap bound through low-dimensional representations.

fits_no_version.finding: Proposition 6 bounds the population-risk increase after rank-k approximation of the trained first-layer weights.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: First-layer weights trained in this setting admit rank-k compression with a controlled population-risk increase.

fits_no_version.finding: Theorem 4 establishes an excess-risk guarantee for monotone single-index targets using sequential training of the two layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: With the specified initialization and training procedure, ReLU networks learn the stated Gaussian single-index targets with sample complexity nearly linear in input dimension.

record.problems: The results rely on Gaussian inputs and a teacher–student setup; the authors state that their learnability guarantee is for single-index models and that simultaneous training of both layers is left for future work. The generalization-gap result is a bound, not an empirical evaluation of the claim’s natural-label versus random-label setting.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant reported results were left out. Other theoretical results concern principal-subspace convergence and learning or compressibility bounds but do not measure the listed versions.

untested.parts: Coexistence of random-label fitting and natural-label generalization, including chance held-out accuracy with random labels.
Actual test-error changes when widening beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image-classification performance and the role of local connectivity or initialization.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer performance under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that recover performance.
Dropout effects on held-out error across data sizes and regularization settings.
Magnitude-aware sharpness correlations with generalization gaps and comparisons with other measures.
Test-accuracy effects of removing memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: Theoretical results can test a version, but these bounds address different propositions. Figures 1–2 illustrate subspace alignment with versus without weight decay and supply no additional result on V1–V8.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out natural-label performance.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold and resulting test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Adaptive optimizer comparisons and held-out performance.
Large-batch comparisons under fixed epoch budgets.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its ranking against other measures.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring test accuracy.

rows.note: The authors state the bound is independent of network width m. This is a theoretical upper bound, not a measured training–test error difference.
rows.check: Theorem 5 is an upper bound, not an observed effect for any version. Correct the value to τ r_a [√(κ(d + log(1/δ))/(γ²T)) + (r_b + λ̃⁻¹)√(dk/T)]; the extracted expression omits τ r_a from the second term. The sufficient sample-size condition also depends logarithmically on m, although the displayed bound does not.

rows.check: The excess-risk guarantee is not a test of any listed version. Its decreasing width-dependent term does not establish actual test-error improvement after zero training error. Theorem 4 also uses a special initialization with identical first-layer neurons and positive second-layer weights and biases.
